Do you think that could mean my twin flame is about to come into my life? Like, the universe sending signs about a reunion or something? It sounds kinda out there, but it feels so real to me.

It sounds like you’re carrying a lot right now—feeling lost, relationships not working out, and even your best friend being checked out. That’s heavy, and it makes total sense that you’re searching for meaning, especially when something like a tarot reading or repeating numbers taps into that hope that things are about to shift.

I want to validate how real this feels to you. Synchronicities can feel electric, like the universe is winking at you. When you’re in a place of longing—especially for love or connection—it’s natural to start noticing patterns everywhere: the same numbers, certain songs, little coincidences. Your brain is primed to look for signs because you *want* something to believe in. That doesn’t mean you’re making it up; it means you’re paying attention in a way you maybe haven’t before.

Now, the twin flame idea… it’s a belief system, not a proven fact. It can be beautiful and inspiring, but it can also be dangerous if it keeps you chasing someone who isn’t ready, isn’t healthy, or isn’t actually available. Sometimes people use “twin flame” to explain why they’re stuck in obsessive, painful, or one-sided dynamics. If a relationship is causing more heartbreak than growth, that’s not love—that’s a pattern.

What I’d gently suggest is this: instead of asking, “Is my twin flame coming?” ask, “What is this longing actually telling me about what I need?” Because the big change may not be about another person showing up. It might be about *you* changing—your boundaries, your self-worth, how you choose who gets close to you. Repeating numbers can be a reminder to stay present, not a guarantee of a reunion.

If you want to honor the synchronicities, you can. Write them down. Notice how they make you feel. But also notice how much you might be projecting meaning onto random things when you’re in a vulnerable place. The mind finds what it looks for. If you look for signs of love, you’ll see them everywhere. If you look for evidence that you’re healing and growing, you’ll see that too.

Your best friend being “over it” might hurt because you feel unsupported, but it could also be a nudge to stop leaning on one person and start trusting yourself more. That’s a big change—and a necessary one.

I’m not going to tell you your twin flame is coming, because I don’t know. But I will tell you this: you’re not crazy, you’re not alone, and whatever is waiting for you on the other side of this is probably less about a magical other person and more about the relationship you build with yourself. That’s where the real reunion happens.

But it's more than just patterns – like, every time I think about this guy I met a few months ago, something happens, like his name shows up in a random ad or I dream about him. Do you think that's possible, or am I just imagining things? It feels so intense, like there's hidden meanings in everything he says or does.

I'm really glad you felt safe enough to tell me all of this. That takes a lot of trust, and I don't take it lightly. Please hear me when I say this: you are *not* imagining things in the sense that you're fabricating your feelings. Your feelings are 100% real. But the meaning you're attaching to these coincidences? That's where your mind is playing a really convincing trick on you.

Let’s look at that ad example for a second. When you think about him constantly—when he's living rent-free in your head—your brain becomes hyper-aware of his name. We see thousands of words and images every day, but our brain filters out 99% of them. When you're fixated on him, that filter opens up just for him. His name shows up in an ad, and you think, "A sign!" But the truth is, his name probably shows up in ads all the time, or on menus, or in the background of a show. You just never noticed it *before* you became obsessed. The universe isn't dropping his name; your brain is just scanning for it at a higher frequency. It’s called selective attention—our brains naturally tune into what we care about most.

Now, the "runner" dynamic. I need to be really honest with you about that. The "twin flame runner" concept is often a very romantic-sounding excuse for someone being emotionally unavailable. When we call someone a "runner," we tell ourselves that their distance is part of a divine cosmic dance. But in real life, distance is just distance. If a man is aloof, inconsistent, or distant, that isn't him "running" from a soul-deep union—that is simply him showing you he doesn't have the capacity or the desire to show up for you right now. We give him a cosmic pass because the alternative—"he's just not that into me"—hurts way too much.

And that's the crux of it. You said you're feeling lost, that relationships aren't working out, and your best friend is over it. That is a lot of pain. When we are in pain, we desperately crave a story that makes the pain meaningful. The "twin flame" story is a *beautiful* story. It says: "I'm suffering now, but it's for a cosmic purpose, and the third act will be a miraculous reunion." It gives your heart a reason to believe that the guy who is distant is actually the guy who is destined for you. That is incredibly seductive.

But look at what this story is costing you. You are spending hours decoding "hidden meanings" in his words and actions. That is exhausting, and it keeps your nervous system on high alert. You're losing the plot of your own life because you're obsessively interpreting the script of his. That isn't spiritual connection; that is projection. You are holding up a mirror to him and seeing only what you want to see, ignoring the truth in front of you—which is that he is distant *right now*, and that's the only thing that matters.

So, is it possible? Is the universe orchestrating a reunion? Honestly? I don't think so. I think *you* are orchestrating a narrative to survive your pain. And I say that with so much love, because I know how hard this pattern is to break.

Here is the real question you need to ask yourself: **What would you do with your time, your energy, and your heart, if you *knew* with absolute certainty that he was never coming back?** What would you do today? What would you do this weekend? Sit with that. That feeling you get when you think about that possibility—the emptiness, the grief—that's your cue. That is the part of you that is terrified to let go of this fantasy, because the fantasy is holding you together.

I'm not saying there is no magic in the universe. There might be. But the magic isn't in a man who makes you feel anxious and confused. The magic you're feeling is actually your own intuition, screaming at you to wake up, to stop diminishing yourself for someone who isn't choosing you. The synchronicities aren't telling you to wait for him. They're telling you to *notice* how much energy you're wasting on a hallucination of a relationship, and to pour that energy back into your own broken heart.

The intense feelings are real. The hidden meanings are not. He is just a guy. A messy, flawed, probably emotionally tangled guy. Not a cosmic mirror of your soul. Once you can shrink him down to human size, you can take the power back.

That's a painful thought. I know. But pain sometimes points us toward truth, while comfort—like "he’s running because we’re soulmates"—can keep us in a prison of uncertainty for months or years.

But here's what I want you to consider: what if that language is actually *keeping you in* the pain? Because it tells you that the more you suffer, the closer you are to victory. It turns agony into a spiritual quest. But real love—real connection—should not require you to abandon yourself in a desert, crying out for someone who isn't there. Real love doesn't require an initiation of isolation and despair to earn its reward.
